topic: How to give feedback that changes behaviour, not just feelings
scope_note: Workplace feedback between peers or from manager to direct report, one-to-one and spoken. Covers behaviour, effect and request with follow-up. Not performance reviews, formal discipline or written feedback.

facts.statement: Feedback is information given to a person about something they did, so that they can decide what to do next time.
Vague feedback such as 'be more professional' gives the listener a judgement but no action they can repeat, stop or change.
facts.caveat: This is broadly accepted practitioner and research consensus, not a precise measured effect. Say it as a common pattern, not a law.

facts.statement: Feedback about a person's character or traits, such as 'you are careless', is easier to take as an attack than feedback about one specific action.
facts.caveat: Reactions vary by person, relationship and context. Say 'often' rather than 'always'.

facts.statement: A listener can nod and agree with vague feedback and still not know what to do differently.
facts.caveat: Agreement in the moment is a weak sign that anything will change.

facts.statement: Observable behaviour is what a camera or any person watching would have seen or heard, such as what was said, when, and to whom.
Judgements about attitude, motive or intent, such as 'you don't care' or 'you were being dismissive', are interpretations, not observations, and the speaker can be wrong about them.
Good feedback names a specific moment, for example 'in today's meeting, you interrupted Sam twice while she was presenting', instead of a general label.
facts.caveat: The example wording is an illustration written for this lesson, not a quotation from any source.

facts.statement: Describing the effect of a behaviour on the team or the work tells the listener why it matters beyond the speaker's opinion.
facts.caveat: Describe effects that actually happened or that you directly felt, and do not speculate about what others think.

facts.statement: Describing your own reaction as a stated effect, such as 'I lost track of the point', is more honest and harder to dispute than claiming to know what others felt or intended.
facts.caveat: This is practitioner guidance, not a tested rule.

facts.statement: A clear request names a specific action for next time, such as 'next meeting, please let her finish before you respond'.
facts.caveat: Example wording is illustrative, written for this lesson.

facts.statement: Feedback that only says what to stop leaves a gap, so a request is stronger when it also says what to do instead.
facts.caveat: Practitioner guidance; sometimes a person needs to be asked what they would do instead.

facts.statement: Agreeing a way to check back, such as a time or a moment when you will talk again, makes it more likely the request is remembered and noticed.
facts.caveat: Phrase as 'more likely', not as guaranteed.

facts.statement: Behaviour, effect and request is one common three-part way to structure feedback, and other models with different names and parts exist and are also used.
facts.caveat: Present this as one useful shape, not the only valid one.

facts.statement: Kind tone alone does not make feedback effective, because tone shapes how it feels while content decides whether the listener knows what to change.
facts.caveat: Tone still matters for the relationship. The point is that it is not sufficient.

facts.statement: Feedback is most useful when given soon after the event, while both people remember the moment clearly.
facts.caveat: Occasionally waiting for calm or privacy is wiser than speaking immediately.

not_claimed: Any percentage or statistic about how much feedback improves performance, or how many people dislike feedback
Any claim that a fixed ratio of positive to negative comments is required
The 'feedback sandwich' is not claimed to be proven best or worst
Any claim that people have learning styles that change how they should receive feedback
Any named expert or quote about feedback
Any claim that one named model is the only correct one
Any claim that this structure guarantees the colleague will change

review.note: Written without sources in topic mode. No numbers and no named studies are used. Needs human review.
